# Indriyabhāvanā Sutta (MN 152 (PTS MN iii 298))
**ID:** MN 152 (PTS MN iii 298)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Indriyabhāvanā Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Development of the Faculties
**PTS:** MN iii 298
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn152

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Indriyabhāvanā Sutta* (MN 152) is the final discourse of the *Majjhima Nikāya*, delivered while the Buddha was staying at Kajangalā in a grove of mukhelu trees [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discourse opens with a dialogue between the Buddha and the young brahmin student Uttara, a pupil of Pārāsariya (or Pārāsiya) [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2017; Polak 2011]. When asked how his teacher instructs disciples in the cultivation of the sense faculties (*indriyabhāvanā*), Uttara explains that one simply avoids seeing forms with the eye and hearing sounds with the ear [Hazra 1994; Anālayo 2017; Polak 2011]. The Buddha responds critically that, by such a standard, the blind and the deaf would be accomplished masters of sensory cultivation [Hazra 1994; Anālayo 2017; Anālayo 2019]. Following this, Ānanda intervenes—marking his final appearance in the *Majjhima Nikāya*—and requests that the Buddha expound the noble cultivation of the faculties [Freedman 1977].
In response, the Buddha explains the "supreme development of the faculties" (*anuttarā indriyabhāvanā*) and the arahant's mastery over perceptions [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Wen]. Rather than attempting the suppression or stoppage of sensory perception, noble cultivation entails experiencing sensory contact at the six sense doors without reactivity: recognizing liking or disliking as conditioned and dependently arisen, quickly abandoning them, and establishing unshakeable equanimity (*upekkhā*) [Polak 2011; Wen].
A full parallel is extant in Chinese translation in the *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 282), alongside Sanskrit fragments identified as SHT sutta70 [SuttaCentral]. Anālayo notes that while the Pali discourse has the Buddha present both the blind and deaf counter-examples, SĀ 282 depicts Ānanda stepping in to supply the example of the deaf [Anālayo 2017]. The discourse is also cited in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (*Iddhikathā*, Ps 3.2) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus reflects this connection, recording close Pali-internal reuse between MN 152 (§16.6–16.10) and Ps 3.2 (§19.2–19.11), as well as significant textual reuse with the *Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta* (SN 35), *Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta* (SN 46), and *Aṅguttara Nikāya* collections (AN 5, AN 6, AN 8, AN 10) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus confirms machine alignment with the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) and several Tibetan canonical works [DharmaNexus].
